column2: Translation of Satie's little play (performed only once in Paris) by M. C. Richards for Cage. Fuller: Baron Medusa, a W. C. Fields–style aristocrat speaking in non sequiturs; Elaine: his daughter Frisette (her only lines: “Yes, Papa”); the handsomest student, William Schrauger: the mute suitor; Isaac Rosenfeld: the gruff butler; Arthur Penn directing; Cage at the piano, Cunningham dancing the entr'actes as the “expensive mechanical monkey.” Elaine designs sets and costumes; Bill turns a large desk and two columns into pink and gray marble with a technique learned at sixteen from a decorator in Holland. Students put in charge of oversized props a month ahead. Mary Outten sews a white Victorian dress from gauze bought in town at 60 cents a yard, and strips of gray satin onto Bucky's khaki trousers.
Building and collapse of the Supine Dome

One damp morning, after long calculations (precomputer), dozens of cheap, flexible Venetian-blind slats are assembled as the framework of a geodesic dome meant to stand twenty-two feet high; the dome does not rise and is affectionately christened the “Supine Dome.” Fuller knew that the slats had to be doubled but went ahead with insufficient materials to demonstrate progressive construction.
Elaine de Kooning paints at Black Mountain
Elaine de Kooning makes paintings during her 1948 stay at Black Mountain, attested retrospectively by the exhibition “Black Mountain Paintings from 1948.”
Cage brings nearly all eighteen existing Satie scores and the composer's only play, The Ruse of Medusa, and proposes an “amateur festival” of Satie's music.
Weil and Rauschenberg enter Black Mountain
In fall 1948, Rauschenberg follows Weil to the United States; both enter Black Mountain, which then has only about a hundred students.
Rauschenberg and Susan Weil enroll at Black Mountain College
Rauschenberg and Susan Weil, an artist and his future wife, enroll at Black Mountain to study with Josef Albers and his Werklehre method, developed at the Bauhaus.
Anni Albers writes to Ted Dreier (letter preserved in the archives of the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation, Albers-Dreier correspondence, box 2, folder 17).
First postwar exhibition in Germany (Galerie Herbert Herrmann, Stuttgart); reluctantly accepts the rectorship of BMC in crisis (faculty and funding).
Albers's funding appeal to the Whitney Foundation

He sets out his reorganization plan: abandon the full liberal arts curriculum (30 teachers needed) to concentrate on the arts and music, supplemented by selected academic subjects and practical work (woodworking, painting, bookbinding, construction for architecture students, farming).
Paris, Académie Julian, meeting Susan Weil

Leaves for Paris; dissatisfied with the teaching and the students' apathy, spends his time with Susan Weil visiting galleries, where he discovers Matisse and Picasso. Paints passionately, often without brushes, with his hands.
Rauschenberg a student at Black Mountain under Albers

First semester: Albers is especially hard on Rauschenberg, who calls himself his dunce; Rauschenberg meets Cage (course on the structure of music and choreography) and Cunningham (modern dance workshop); inseparable from Weil, whom Albers nicknames, with him, the Bobbsey twins
Study in Paris, Académie Julian, with Susan Weil
Paris, Académie Julian and boardinghouse

After a year in Kansas, he sails for Paris on a converted troopship: a city not recovered from the war, a disappointing Académie Julian, and meeting Susan Weil, another art student; he often paints with his hands, palms, and fists in their boardinghouse room.
A summer of study in Paris

After high school, Weil spends the summer in Paris: painting at the Académie Julian, drawing at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière. There she meets Rauschenberg, in the same boardinghouse and the same art and French classes.
Rauschenberg and Susan Weil meet in Paris

Both enrolled in art classes at the Académie Julian; Weil is 18, six years younger than Rauschenberg; she helps him find his way and leads him to Black Mountain, which she had visited as a high school student, determined to study with Josef Albers
Rauschenberg's period of study in Paris
A period of study at the Académie Julian, cradle of the Nabis, described as unrewarding; he does not frequent the postwar Paris Surrealist group there.
Fascinated by a Time article (August issue) on Josef Albers's pictorial discipline, he decides to return to the United States in the fall to study at Black Mountain College, where Albers teaches.
Black Mountain College, near Asheville, North Carolina
1948 summer session: Cage, Cunningham, de Kooning, Fuller, Lippold, Newhall

About twenty rotating teachers from July to August 1948: Cunningham and Cage (visitors earlier in the year, invited back), de Kooning and Lippold recommended by Cage, Fuller, Newhall (already in residence in summer 1946, back to teach the history of photography). The session surpasses that of 1946 in popularity and scope.

Black Mountain College, under the trees
The de Koonings' stay at Black Mountain College

On the strength of his success at Egan's, de Kooning is invited by Josef Albers to join for the summer a faculty that includes John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Buckminster Fuller, and Richard Lippold. During this rural stay, Elaine reads passages of Kierkegaard to Bill — a memory of Patricia Passlof's.
